captions.text: A fraction tells you about a particular whole.
When the whole changes, the same fraction can describe
a different number of pieces.
Draw equal parts for the first whole, then mark which
amount becomes the whole for the next instruction.
In AMC practice, a fraction of the original pile and a
fraction of what is left can occur in the same problem.
Underline the words after of.
A Rossmoyne style word puzzle may reveal the ending and
ask you to recover the starting quantity.
Reverse one change at a time.
There are fifteen tokens.
A player takes one of three equal parts.
How many tokens remain?
Show the difference between the amount removed and the
amount the question asks for.
One part has five tokens.
The remaining two parts contain ten tokens.
Check by adding the removed part back.
ten plus five returns fifteen.
A box starts with thirty chalk pieces.
A class uses one of three equal parts.
Then another class uses one of two equal parts of what
is left.
How many pieces remain after both classes?
Label the whole for each fraction.
After the first class the remaining count is twenty,
since thirty divided by three were used.
The next whole is now twenty.
Divide it into two equal parts.
The second class uses ten pieces.
Subtract the second use to get ten.
This is one of the second whole's parts.
Take one of three equal parts from a pile.
Add a gift of four pieces.
Then take one of two equal parts of that new amount.
There are twelve pieces left.
How many were in the original pile?
The ending twelve pieces represent one of the last two
equal parts.
Find one part, then rebuild that whole.
Undo the gift by subtracting four.
The remaining twenty pieces are what was left after the
first removal.
Those were two of the original three equal parts.
Restoring the missing part gives thirty.
Run the recipe forward.
Remove ten from thirty to get twenty.
Add the gift to get twenty-four.
The final removal is twelve.
That leaves twelve, the stated ending.
Each fraction has used its own whole.
Add fractions directly only when they refer to the same
original whole.
A fraction of what is left uses a new whole.
When reversing a removal, divide the remaining amount
by the number of remaining parts first.
The denominator names the size of the full set of
parts.
Write the word original, remaining or new above each
fraction.
Draw equal parts for that named whole.
If the ending is known, rebuild the last whole first.
Then reverse any addition and earlier removal.
